chapters.title: Chapter 3: What Sits on Top of the Slabs

lessons.title: Marginal Relief Just Above the Rebate Threshold

body.text: Marginal relief stops a ₹1 raise from costing you ₹60,000 of tax. Just above ₹12 lakh, your tax before cess can never exceed the income you earned above ₹12 lakh.

children.text: The rebate you met in the last lesson has a hard edge. At Total Income of ₹12,00,000 a resident pays nothing. At ₹12,00,100, with no rebate at all, slab tax would be ₹60,015, meaning ₹100 of extra income triggers ₹60,015 of tax. No sensible tax system can work like that, so the new regime adds marginal relief to smooth the edge.

body.label: Where Marginal Relief Lives
body.value: Proviso to section 156, Income-tax Act, 2025 (proviso to section 87A, Income-tax Act, 1961)
body.context: Available only under the new regime, only to resident individuals, and only for Total Income slightly above ₹12 lakh. The old regime has no equivalent at ₹5 lakh.

children.text: If a resident individual's Total Income under the new regime exceeds ₹12,00,000, the tax payable on it, before cess, is limited to the amount by which the income exceeds ₹12,00,000. You pay the lower of normal slab tax and that excess. The difference is the marginal relief.

body.latex: \text{Tax before cess} = \min\big(\,\text{Slab Tax},\ \text{Total Income} - 12{,}00{,}000\,\big) \qquad \text{Marginal Relief} = \text{Slab Tax} - \text{Tax before cess}
body.caption: For resident individuals under the new regime with only slab-rate income above ₹12 lakh

children.text: Let E be the income above ₹12 lakh. Slab tax is ₹60,000 plus 15% of E. Relief applies while the excess E is smaller than slab tax, and stops once they are equal.

body.caption: Marginal relief applies for Total Income from ₹12,00,001 to about ₹12,70,588
Marginal Relief in Action, Resident, New Regime, Slab-Rate Income Only

body.title: Tax Before Cess Around ₹12 Lakh: With and Without Marginal Relief

children.text: Without relief, the tax line jumps vertically from zero to over ₹60,000 at ₹12 lakh. With relief, it climbs diagonally, rupee for rupee with the excess income, until it meets the normal slab tax line at about ₹12.7 lakh and then follows it.
The Catch: Cess Makes the Zone a Small Loss

Marginal relief caps tax before cess at the excess income. But the 4% cess is then added on top. So inside the relief zone, every extra rupee costs ₹1.04 of tax, a marginal rate of 104%. Your take-home income actually falls slightly as you earn more, until normal slab tax takes over and you climb back.

body.caption: Income Left After Tax Around ₹12 Lakh

body.title: Show me the math: where take-home recovers

children.text: Inside the relief zone, income after tax is ₹12,00,000 + E − 1.04E = ₹12,00,000 − 0.04E, which is always below ₹12 lakh. The worst point is at the end of the zone, E ≈ ₹70,588, where you are about ₹2,824 worse off. Beyond the zone, income after tax is ₹12,00,000 + E − 1.04 × (₹60,000 + 0.15E) = ₹12,00,000 + 0.844E − ₹62,400. This gets back to ₹12,00,000 when 0.844E = ₹62,400, so E ≈ ₹73,933.6, a Total Income of about ₹12,73,934.

body.text: Keep the loss in perspective. Without marginal relief, a resident at ₹12,10,000 would pay ₹63,960 including cess. With relief they pay ₹10,400. The worst-case loss inside the zone is under ₹3,000. Marginal relief does not make the zone free, but it turns a ₹60,000 cliff into a small dip.

children.text: Using the Zone to Your Advantage

Because the marginal rate inside the zone is 104%, any allowed deduction that brings Total Income back to ₹12 lakh saves more tax than its own size. Under the new regime, the main lever for salaried employees is the employer NPS contribution. Every rupee moved from taxable salary into employer NPS removes ₹1.04 of tax until you are back at ₹12 lakh.

body.text: These figures assume all income is taxed at slab rates. If you have special-rate income, such as short-term gains on shares, the calculation changes: that income counts towards the ₹12 lakh limit, the rebate does not apply to tax on it, and the relief computation must be done carefully. The ITR utility on incometax.gov.in applies the relief automatically, but check its result against your own working.

body.title: Am I in the Marginal Relief Zone?
steps: Confirm you are a resident individual under the new regime
Compute Total Income. If it is ₹12,00,000 or less, the rebate applies and marginal relief is irrelevant
If it is above ₹12,00,000, compute normal slab tax and the excess over ₹12,00,000
Pay the lower of the two before cess; the difference is your marginal relief
If your Total Income is between ₹12,00,001 and roughly ₹12,74,000, look for an allowed deduction, such as employer NPS, that brings you back to ₹12 lakh

body.title: Calculate the Marginal Relief
body.prompt: Shweta, a resident HR manager in Bhubaneswar, is on the new regime with Total Income of ₹12,40,000, all from salary. How much marginal relief does she get?
body.explanation: Slab tax is ₹60,000 + 15% of ₹40,000 = ₹66,000. The excess over ₹12 lakh is ₹40,000. Tax before cess is limited to ₹40,000, so marginal relief is ₹66,000 − ₹40,000 = ₹26,000. With cess, she pays ₹41,600.

body.title: Just Outside the Zone?
body.question: Imran, a resident on the new regime, has Total Income of ₹12,80,000, all from salary. What is his tax including 4% cess?
body.explanation: Slab tax is ₹60,000 + 15% of ₹80,000 = ₹72,000. The excess is ₹80,000, which is higher than slab tax, so marginal relief gives nothing and normal slab tax applies. ₹72,000 plus 4% cess of ₹2,880 is ₹74,880. Imran is past the end of the zone at about ₹12,70,588.

body.title: The Relief Rule
body.textWithBlank: Under marginal relief, a resident's tax before cess cannot exceed the amount by which Total Income exceeds ₹___.
body.explanation: The rebate limit is ₹12,00,000. Marginal relief ensures that the tax on income just above it is never more than the extra income itself, before the 4% cess.

body.title: Should Rahul Bother With NPS?
body.scenario: Rahul, a resident sales manager in Ahmedabad, is on the new regime. His basic salary is ₹5,00,000 and his Total Income for tax year 2026-27 is projected at ₹12,60,000, all salary. HR allows employer NPS contributions of up to 14% of basic. A colleague says: "You're only ₹60,000 over the limit, marginal relief protects you, so don't bother with NPS."
body.prompt: Is the colleague right? Compare Rahul's tax with and without a ₹60,000 employer NPS contribution, and state any trade-off.
body.modelAnswer: The colleague is only partly right. Marginal relief does protect Rahul from paying full slab tax of ₹69,000, but he still pays tax equal to his entire ₹60,000 excess, plus ₹2,400 of cess: ₹62,400. His 14% NPS limit is ₹70,000, so a ₹60,000 employer NPS contribution is allowed. It brings Total Income to exactly ₹12,00,000, the rebate cancels all tax, and he pays zero. He saves ₹62,400 by setting aside ₹60,000 for retirement. The trade-off is liquidity: NPS money is largely locked in until age 60.

points: Marginal relief applies to resident individuals under the new regime with Total Income slightly above ₹12 lakh
Tax before cess is capped at the income in excess of ₹12 lakh; the difference from slab tax is the relief
The relief zone runs from ₹12,00,001 to about ₹12,70,588, where slab tax catches up with the excess
Because cess is added after the cap, the marginal rate inside the zone is 104% and take-home dips by up to about ₹2,800
Take-home returns above the ₹12 lakh level only at Total Income of about ₹12,74,000
Inside the zone, an allowed deduction such as employer NPS can save more tax than its own amount
The old regime has no marginal relief at its ₹5 lakh rebate limit

body.text: Figures assume a resident individual under the new regime for tax year 2026-27 with only slab-rate income. Special-rate income and surcharge change the computation. This lesson is for education only and is not tax advice.
